questions.stem: Prove that among any $5$ points on a segment of length $1$, two are at distance at most $\frac{1}{4}$.

hint.level_0: Cut the segment into $n$ equal pieces.
hint.level_1: Pigeonhole the points.

solution_steps: Split the unit segment into $4$ pieces each of length $\tfrac1{4}$.
With $5$ points and $4$ pieces, two share a piece (pigeonhole).
Two points in one piece are within its length $\tfrac1n$.

questions.stem: Prove that among any $5$ points with integer coordinates, two have a midpoint that also has integer coordinates.

hint.level_1: How many parity classes are there?

solution_steps: Classify each point by the parities $(x\bmod2,\,y\bmod2)$ of its coordinates.
There are only $2\times2=4$ parity classes.
With $5$ points, two share a class (pigeonhole).
For those two, $x$-coordinates have equal parity and likewise $y$, so their midpoint is integral.

questions.stem: Prove that among any $5$ points in a unit square, two are at distance at most $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

hint.level_0: Divide the square into four cells.
hint.level_1: Diagonal of a half-square.

solution_steps: Cut the unit square into $4$ congruent sub-squares of side $\tfrac12$.
With $5$ points and $4$ cells, two points lie in the same cell (pigeonhole).
The largest distance within a $\tfrac12$-square is its diagonal $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.
Hence those two points are at distance $\le\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

questions.stem: Prove the Happy Ending theorem for $n=4$: any $5$ points in general position (no three collinear) contain $4$ that form a convex quadrilateral.

hint.level_0: Look at the convex hull's size.
hint.level_1: If it's a triangle, use the line through the two interior points.

solution_steps: Consider the convex hull of the $5$ points. If it has $4$ or $5$ vertices, pick any $4$ hull vertices.
Otherwise the hull is a triangle $ABC$ with the other two points $D,E$ inside.
Line $DE$ leaves two of $A,B,C$ on one side (pigeonhole); say $A,B$.
Then $A,B,D,E$ form a convex quadrilateral.

questions.stem: Prove Radon's theorem in the plane: any $4$ points can be split into two groups whose convex hulls intersect.

hint.level_0: Two cases: one point inside, or convex quadrilateral.
hint.level_1: Use the diagonals in the convex case.

solution_steps: If one point lies inside the triangle of the other three, that point vs.\ the triangle is a Radon partition.
Otherwise the four points are in convex position, forming a quadrilateral.
Its two diagonals cross, so the two pairs of opposite vertices have intersecting hulls.
Either way the required partition exists.

questions.stem: Prove Carath\'eodory's theorem in the plane: if a point $P$ lies in the convex hull of a set $S\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, then $P$ lies in the convex hull of at most $3$ points of $S$.

hint.level_1: Four points in the plane are affinely dependent.

solution_steps: $P$ is a convex combination of some points of $S$; take one using the fewest points, say $k$.
If $k\ge4$, those $k$ points are affinely dependent in the plane (any $4$ points in $\mathbb R^2$ are).
The dependence lets us cancel one point from the combination while keeping it convex.
This contradicts minimality, so $k\le3$.

questions.stem: Prove that $3$ lines in general position (no two parallel, no three concurrent) determine exactly $\binom{3}{2}=3$ intersection points.

hint.level_1: General position makes the correspondence a bijection.

solution_steps: Each pair of lines meets in exactly one point (no two are parallel).
Different pairs give different points (no three lines are concurrent).
So the number of intersection points equals the number of pairs, $\binom{3}{2}=3$.

questions.stem: Prove that $3$ lines in general position divide the plane into $1+3+\binom{3}{2}=7$ regions.

hint.level_1: The $k$-th line is cut into $k$ pieces.

solution_steps: Add the lines one at a time. With no lines there is $1$ region.
The $k$-th line meets the previous $k-1$ lines in $k-1$ points, which cut it into $k$ pieces.
Each piece splits an existing region in two, adding $k$ regions.
Total: $1+\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=1+n+\binom{n}{2}=7$.

questions.stem: Prove that a lattice triangle with no lattice points other than its $3$ vertices has area exactly $\tfrac12$.

hint.level_1: Or pair it into a unit-area parallelogram.

solution_steps: Such a triangle has $I=0$ interior and $B=3$ boundary lattice points.
By Pick's theorem $A=I+\tfrac B2-1=0+\tfrac32-1=\tfrac12$.
(Independently: two copies tile a fundamental parallelogram of the integer lattice, area $1$.)

questions.stem: For the lattice polygon with vertices [[0, 0], [4, 0], [0, 3]], verify and prove Pick's theorem $A=I+\frac{B}{2}-1$ (here $A=6$, $I=3$, $B=8$).

hint.level_0: Prove it for a primitive triangle first.
hint.level_1: Show both sides add over a shared edge.

solution_steps: Pick's theorem holds for a single lattice triangle of area $\tfrac12$ (it has $I=0,B=3$).
Both sides of $A=I+\tfrac B2-1$ are additive when two lattice polygons are glued along a common edge.
Triangulating the polygon into primitive (area-$\tfrac12$) triangles and adding up gives the formula.
Here $I=3$, $B=8$, so $I+\tfrac B2-1=6=A$.

questions.stem: Prove Blichfeldt's theorem: any bounded region in the plane of area greater than $1$ contains two distinct points whose difference is a vector with integer coordinates.

hint.level_0: Fold the region into the unit square.
hint.level_1: Area $>1$ forces an overlap.

solution_steps: Cut the plane into the unit cells $[m,m+1)\times[k,k+1)$ and translate each piece of the region back into $[0,1)^2$.
The total area $>1$ is packed into the unit square, so two pieces overlap (a measure/pigeonhole argument).
An overlap point comes from two region points $P,Q$ that were translated by different integer vectors.
Then $P-Q$ has integer coordinates, as required.

questions.stem: Prove that the interior angles of a convex $4$-gon sum to $(4-2)\cdot180^\circ=360^\circ$.

hint.level_1: Count the triangles.

solution_steps: Triangulate the polygon from one vertex into $n-2$ triangles.
The triangles' angles together make up exactly the polygon's interior angles.
Each triangle contributes $180^\circ$, so the total is $(n-2)180^\circ=360^\circ$.

questions.stem: Prove that every triangulation of a convex $4$-gon uses exactly $4-2=2$ triangles and $4-3=1$ diagonals.

hint.level_1: Count edge incidences for the diagonal count.

solution_steps: The interior angles of the polygon sum to $(n-2)\cdot180^\circ$.
Each triangle contributes $180^\circ$ of angle, and all angle is accounted for.
So the number of triangles is $\frac{(n-2)180^\circ}{180^\circ}=n-2$.
Each triangle has $3$ edges; counting edge-incidences ($3(n-2)=$ sides $n$ $+$ $2\times$#diagonals) gives $n-3$ diagonals.

questions.stem: A triangulation of a point set with $I$ interior and $B$ boundary points (boundary in convex position) has exactly $2I+B-2$ triangles. Prove this and check the case $I=1,B=4$.

hint.level_0: Add up all the triangle angles.
hint.level_1: Interior vertices give $360^\circ$ each.

solution_steps: Let $T$ be the number of triangles and $E$ edges. Sum of all triangle angles is $180^\circ T$.
Interior points contribute $360^\circ$ each; boundary points contribute the polygon's angle sum $(B-2)180^\circ$.
So $180^\circ T=360^\circ I+(B-2)180^\circ$, giving $T=2I+B-2$.

questions.stem: Prove Chv\'atal's Art Gallery theorem: $\lfloor n/3\rfloor$ guards always suffice (and are sometimes necessary) to see the whole interior of a simple polygon with $n$ vertices.

hint.level_1: Guard the rarest colour; comb gives the lower bound.

solution_steps: Triangulate the polygon; the resulting graph (vertices + diagonals) is $3$-colourable (its dual is a tree).
Each triangle has one vertex of each colour, so placing guards on the least-used colour class covers every triangle.
That colour class has at most $\lfloor n/3\rfloor$ vertices, so $\lfloor n/3\rfloor$ guards suffice.
A 'comb' polygon with $k$ prongs ($n=3k$) needs $k=\lfloor n/3\rfloor$ guards, proving necessity.

questions.stem: Prove that a set of points in an $3\times 3$ grid with no three collinear has at most $2\cdot3=6$ points.

hint.level_1: A full row of $3$ would be collinear.

solution_steps: Each of the $3$ rows is a line, so it contains at most $2$ of the chosen points.
Summing over the $3$ rows gives at most $2\cdot3=6$ points.
(This bound $2n$ is achieved for small $n$ by explicit 'no-three-in-line' configurations.)

questions.stem: Prove that any $2$-colouring of the $3\times7$ grid of points contains an axis-aligned rectangle whose four corners share a colour.

hint.level_0: In each column find a repeated colour.
hint.level_1: Only $6$ column-types, but $7$ columns.

solution_steps: In each column of $3$ points, two share a colour (pigeonhole).
Record that column's 'type': which colour is repeated and in which of the $\binom{3}{2}=3$ row-pairs.
There are only $2\times3=6$ possible types but $7$ columns.
Two columns share a type; their repeated same-colour cells form a monochromatic rectangle.

questions.stem: Prove Helly's theorem on the line: if finitely many intervals pairwise intersect, then they have a common point.

hint.level_0: Compare the largest left endpoint and smallest right endpoint.
hint.level_1: Pairwise intersection gives $L\le R$.

solution_steps: Let $L=\max_i a_i$ (largest left endpoint) and $R=\min_i b_i$ (smallest right endpoint).
Pick intervals achieving $L$ and $R$; since they intersect, $L\le R$.
Then every interval contains the point $L$ (as $a_i\le L\le R\le b_i$).
So all intervals share the point $L$.

questions.stem: Prove that among $n$ points in the plane, the maximum distance (the diameter) is attained by at most $n$ pairs.

hint.level_0: Two diameter segments cannot be disjoint.
hint.level_1: Bound an intersecting family of edges.

solution_steps: Call a segment realising the diameter $D$ a 'diameter edge'. Two diameter edges must cross or share an endpoint (else two points would be $>D$ apart).
Hence the diameter edges form a graph in which every two edges meet.
Such an 'intersecting' family of segments on $n$ points has at most $n$ edges.
So at most $n$ pairs achieve the diameter.

questions.stem: Prove that the chromatic number of the plane is at least $4$: there is a set of points whose unit-distance graph (the Moser spindle, $7$ points and $11$ unit segments) cannot be properly $3$-coloured.

hint.level_1: Force a contradiction in any $3$-colouring.

solution_steps: Build two rhombi (each two unit equilateral triangles) hinged at a common vertex $O$.
Rotate one rhombus about $O$ until the two far vertices are at unit distance; join them.
This gives $7$ points with $11$ unit-distance edges (the Moser spindle).
A short case-check shows it has no proper $3$-colouring, so the plane needs $\ge4$ colours for unit distances.

questions.stem: Prove the Sylvester--Gallai theorem: for any finite set of points in the plane, not all on a line, there is a line passing through exactly two of them (an 'ordinary' line).

hint.level_1: Use the perpendicular foot and pigeonhole on its sides.

solution_steps: Among all (point, connecting-line) pairs with the point off the line, choose one with the smallest distance $d>0$.
Suppose that line $\ell$ contained $\ge3$ points; drop the perpendicular foot $F$ from the point $P$ to $\ell$.
Two of those $\ge3$ points lie on the same side of $F$; the nearer one is closer to the line $P$-(farther one) than $d$.
This contradicts minimality, so $\ell$ has exactly two points — an ordinary line.

questions.stem: Prove the de Bruijn--Erdős theorem: $n$ points in the plane, not all collinear, determine at least $n$ distinct lines.

hint.level_0: Use Sylvester--Gallai to find an ordinary line.
hint.level_1: Induct on the number of points.

solution_steps: Induct on $n$. Remove a point $P$ that lies on an ordinary line (exists by Sylvester--Gallai).
The remaining $n-1$ points, if not all collinear, determine $\ge n-1$ lines by induction.
Re-adding $P$: the ordinary line through $P$ is new, giving $\ge n$ lines.
(If the remaining points are collinear, count directly: $n-1$ lines to $P$ plus the common line $=n$.)
